name: Voice-maxxing

card.summary: Working on pitch, resonance and delivery to sound more attractive or masculine; speech-therapy techniques exist, but no trials test it for attractiveness.
card.note: Voice therapy is established for medical use; its use for attractiveness has not been studied in trials.

quick.overview:
Voice-maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of changing how one sounds, most often aiming for a deeper, more resonant voice. Looksmax.org has long-running threads on whether a deep voice raises attractiveness and how to acquire one.

Speech-language pathologists use voice therapy to alter pitch, resonance and voice quality for medical and gender-voice purposes, but no published trial has tested it as an attractiveness intervention.
quick.mechanism: Voice pitch is set largely by vocal fold length and tension, with typical adult male speech around 90 to 155 Hz and female around 165 to 255 Hz. Therapy approaches work on breathing, resonance and pitch habits rather than the anatomy itself.
quick.risks: Training itself is low risk when taught by a clinician; forceful pitch-lowering can strain the voice, and therapy sources emphasise vocal hygiene. Surgical or hormonal changes to the voice are separate medical topics.

lead: Voice-maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of changing how one sounds, most often to sound deeper, more resonant and more confident, so that a person comes across as more attractive, masculine or authoritative. The voice is treated as part of the overall impression alongside face and body: it is heard on calls, in person and on video before and while a person is seen, and the topic is a recurring subject on looksmax.org.[1][2][5]

The routes people describe are technique, delivery and (in puberty) hormones. Technique borrows from speech-language pathology and singing: relaxed breathing from the diaphragm, a relaxed larynx, chest-focused resonance, posture and chin position. Delivery covers pace, volume, intonation and clarity. A forum reply in one thread says most people speak above their natural pitch, so relaxing the cords and breathing from the diaphragm can lower habitual pitch by 5 to 10 Hz.[6][2]

Typical adult male speech has a fundamental frequency of about 90 to 155 Hz and typical adult female speech about 165 to 255 Hz.[3] Scientific interest in voice and attractiveness is substantial: multiple studies reviewed below report that women on average rate lower-pitched men's voices as more attractive and masculine, though the preference varies by context, cycle phase and the pitch range tested, and very low voices were not preferred in at least one experiment.[10][11][12][14] Voice therapy by speech-language pathologists is an established clinical field for voice disorders and gender-voice work, though no published trial has tested it as an attractiveness intervention.[4]

Male voice deepens about an octave in puberty[7]

paras: Voice-maxxing discussions centre on pitch (how high or low a voice sounds), resonance (where the voice seems to vibrate: chest, throat or face), and delivery. Clinical sources describe resonant voice as felt higher and more forward, around the alveolar ridge and maxillary bones, and this is a common target in feminising voice work.[4] Forum members talk about the opposite, chest resonance, for masculinising.[6][2]
Phonetic references add that listeners perceive a pitch even when the lowest harmonic is faint, the missing-fundamental effect.[3]

Air from the lungs sets the vocal folds vibrating; the throat, mouth and nasal cavities then shape the sound. Pitch is tied to the vibration rate of the folds, which laryngeal muscles adjust through length and tension.[9] Adult male vocal folds are about 17 to 25 mm long versus about 12.5 to 17.5 mm in women, and men also generally have a larger vocal tract, which lowers timbre largely independently of the folds.[9]

Resonance cavities include the chest, larynx, nasal cavity and sinuses, and individual variation comes from body size, bone structure and vocal tract shape.[9] This is the physical basis for the claim that technique can change how deep a voice sounds without altering the folds themselves: changing breathing, laryngeal position and resonance habits shifts timbre and habitual pitch within a person's natural range.[4]

Before puberty boys and girls have roughly similar pitches. During puberty the male voice typically deepens by about an octave while the female voice becomes richer, as sex hormones, mainly testosterone, enlarge the larynx in both sexes, far more in males. The vocal folds lengthen and thicken, and growth of the sinuses, nose and throat adds resonance space.[7] Adult pitch is reached two to three years after changes begin, and the voice stabilises between roughly ages 21 and 25.[7]

Wikipedia also describes the voice crack, a brief unintended jump to a higher register that can result from puberty, stress, fatigue, emotional tension or speaking outside one's natural range.[7] It records the historical practice of preserving unchanged voices through castration, first documented in Italian church records from the 1550s, outlawed in Italy in 1861, with the Pope barring new castrati from the church in 1878.[7]

Threads describe three kinds of approach. The first is technique: relaxing the throat, breathing with the diaphragm, tucking the chin and raising the tongue, and using exercises that members say are taught in gender-voice training videos.[6][2] The second is delivery: speed, volume, intonation and tone of speech. The third is hormonal, with a looksmax.org guide stating that androgens work significantly only during puberty and discussing androgenic drugs for adolescents.[2] This article does not give dosing or sourcing for such compounds.

Clinical voice work offers a parallel vocabulary. Resonant voice therapy teaches voicing with minimally closed vocal folds to reduce force and trauma, moving from humming and nasal sounds to words and conversation. The Accent Method combines diaphragmatic breathing with rhythmic vowel play, typically in 20-minute sessions two to three times a week, and chant-talk uses prolonged vowels and softened word onsets to lower effort.[4] Stretching, resistance and endurance exercises train range, loudness control and stamina.[4] Voice therapy is typically provided by a speech-language pathologist.[9]

Studies of voice and mate choice consistently examine pitch (fundamental frequency, F0), formant dispersion and position (cues to vocal tract length and body size) and loudness. Re and colleagues manipulated pitch in 2 Hz steps in three experiments with 19 university students; women preferred men's voices lowered in pitch, but did not prefer very low men's voices, while men preferred higher-pitched women's voices across the range tested.[10]

Simmons and colleagues reported that women rated lower-pitched men's voices as more masculine and attractive, but pitch did not predict semen quality, and men with more attractive voices tended to have lower sperm concentrations.[11] Suire and colleagues found French-speaking women were more attracted to lower pitch and higher intonation patterns, with no directional preference for several other acoustic features.[12]

Hodges-Simeon and colleagues analysed speech from an unscripted dating game and found women's attractiveness ratings were predicted by low mean pitch, low formant dispersion and high loudness, with low formant dispersion rated attractive only by women in their fertile phase.[17] Feinberg and colleagues reported that women generally preferred masculinised men's voices, more strongly in the fertile late-follicular phase.[14] O'Connor and colleagues, in two studies with 95 and 80 women, found that higher dyadic sexual desire and more positive attitudes toward uncommitted sex predicted stronger preferences for masculine voices, particularly for short-term relationships.[13]

Puts and colleagues found that in US and Hadza samples, voice measures such as formant position related to height and, in the US sample, to upper-body strength, and that F0 predicted testosterone; they interpret masculine voices as signalling men's threat potential.[15] A 2016 paper across anthropoid primates reported that humans show greater male F0 dimorphism than any other ape and that low male F0 predicted perceived dominance and attractiveness, low cortisol and high testosterone.[16] A speed-dating study found men lowered their minimum pitch when speaking with women highly desired by others, and with women they chose.[18]

Not all results point one way. Babel and colleagues found Californian listeners' attractiveness ratings of isolated words depended on apparent talker size and conformity to community speech norms, and that men rated other men as less attractive than women did.[19] McAleer and colleagues reported that listeners' impressions of brief 'hello' utterances fell along valence and dominance dimensions, with higher valence and dominance together raising perceived male vocal attractiveness.[20] These studies describe perceptions of recorded voices, not outcomes of training.

Voice therapy orientations are described as symptomatic, physiologic, hygienic, psychogenic or eclectic, and no single method suits everyone.[4] The literature includes a 2016 systematic review of resonant voice therapy by Yiu and colleagues and a 1991 study of the Accent Method by Kotby and colleagues, both cited in Wikipedia's voice therapy article.[4] Hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery do little to change pitch, which is why voice work is used alongside them in gender-affirming care, and surgical options to alter vocal structure such as cricothyroid approximation are considered after other methods.[4] The WPATH Standards of Care version 8 includes a chapter on voice and communication.[21]

No published study identified here tested whether training to deepen voice pitch changes attractiveness ratings, so the connection between training and appearance-style outcomes is documented in forum reports and inferred from the perception research above.[4][10]

Voice therapy sources emphasise vocal hygiene: avoiding yelling, throat clearing and talking over noise, staying hydrated and limiting alcohol and caffeine.[4] Prolonged improper voice use causes vocal loading, with nodules arising from repeated vocal abuse and polyps usually from a single incident and sometimes needing surgical removal; hoarseness or breathiness lasting more than two weeks should be medically evaluated.[9] Wikipedia notes that people dropping pitch after puberty can strain the voice by forcing it into pitches outside their comfortable range.[7]
Adolescent androgen use discussed in some forum guides is a separate medical topic with its own risks.[2]

Thread titles show members asking how much a deep voice increases sexual market value, whether it is a good halo or noticeable at all, whether raspy or deep is better, and whether a deep voice is optimal for younger men.[1][5][22][23][24] The long-running question 'does a deep voice make you more attractive' appears on looksmax.org in several forms.[25]

Positions run both ways: some members call voice a real attractiveness factor, others argue women prefer higher-pitched voices or that the effect is exaggerated, and some say voice quality and charm matter more than depth alone.[1][5][2] Other posts attribute deep voices to growth hormone rather than testosterone alone.[8] Members also discuss surgery for pitch in replies, which clinical sources treat as a late option for voice-gender work.[2][4]

No studies found on voice-maxxing training for attractiveness. Related research covers listeners' ratings of voice pitch and formants, and clinical voice therapy for medical and gender-voice purposes, as summarised above.[10][4]

timeline.event: Castrati are first documented in Italian church records, preserving unchanged high voices.[7]
Castration for voice preservation becomes illegal in Italy.[7]
Pope Leo XIII prohibits the church from hiring new castrati.[7]
Kotby and colleagues publish a study of the Accent Method for voice therapy.[4]
Feinberg and colleagues report stronger preferences for masculinised voices in the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle.[14]
Hodges-Simeon, Gaulin and Puts analyse which vocal parameters predict attractiveness and dominance in a dating game.[17]
Simmons and colleagues report women rate lower-pitched voices as more attractive but pitch does not predict semen quality.[11]
Re and colleagues test preferences across very low and very high pitch; Puts and colleagues link masculine voices to threat potential.[10][15]
Puts and colleagues report sexual selection on male F0 across anthropoid primates; Yiu and colleagues publish a systematic review of resonant voice therapy.[16][4]
A speed-dating study shows men and women adjust voice pitch toward desired partners.[18]
Suire and colleagues examine French-speaking women's ratings of male voices.[12]
WPATH Standards of Care version 8 includes a voice and communication chapter.[21]

lore.intro: Members debate whether a deep voice is a meaningful attractiveness factor and how to get one; the topic runs from posture and breathing tips to hormonal explanations.[1][2][5][6]

claims.claim: A deep voice makes a man more attractive.
claims.believers: Threads ask how much a deep voice raises attractiveness and call it a halo, with some posters agreeing it matters.[5][22]
claims.experts: Several studies report women rate lower-pitched men's voices as more attractive and masculine, though one experiment found very low voices were not preferred.[10][11][12]

claims.claim: Women prefer higher-pitched voices, so a deep voice is a disadvantage.
claims.believers: At least one thread argues masculine deep voices are a mistake because women prefer higher-pitched voices.[1]
claims.experts: In the Re et al. experiments men preferred higher-pitched women's voices, while women preferred men's voices lowered in pitch.[10]

claims.claim: Relaxing the throat and breathing from the diaphragm can drop pitch by 5-10 Hz.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply says most people speak above their natural pitch and that relaxing the cords and breathing from the diaphragm lowers it by that range.[6]
claims.experts: Voice therapy references describe diaphragmatic breathing and reduced vocal strain as parts of established techniques but report no figures for pitch lowering.[4]

claims.claim: Voice deepening is meaningful mainly during puberty, and androgens during adolescence deepen it.
claims.believers: A voice-maxxing guide says the approach significantly works only in puberty and discusses androgenic compounds for that window.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes puberty-era testosterone enlarging the larynx and lengthening the vocal folds, with the voice stabilising by about 21 to 25.[7]

claims.claim: Deep voice reflects growth hormone, not just testosterone.
claims.believers: A thread title asserts the deep voice is 'growth hormones not just muh testosterone'.[8]
claims.experts: The cited sources describe sex hormones, mainly testosterone, as driving laryngeal growth and do not address growth hormone; Puts and colleagues found F0 predicted testosterone in a US sample.[7][15]

claims.claim: A low voice signals dominance or masculinity to others.
claims.believers: Members describe deep voices as masculine and as a halo.[5]
claims.experts: Puts and colleagues report masculine voice measures relate to height, strength and testosterone and to perceived dominance.[15][16][17]

claims.claim: Voice is read together with other traits, so charm and delivery matter beyond depth.
claims.believers: Posters argue voice quality and charm are not just about depth.[2][5]
claims.experts: McAleer and colleagues found impressions of voices fall along valence and dominance dimensions, and Babel and colleagues found apparent size and conformity to local speech norms predicted attractiveness.[19][20]

angle.text: Forum guides describe lowering habitual pitch by a few hertz through relaxed breathing and resonance work, and attribute larger changes to puberty-era hormones. Practitioners say a deeper voice adds to first impressions on calls, in person and on video, and perception studies report that women on average rate lower-pitched men's voices as more attractive.
